title: Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened
author: Nicole Williams
summary: Nicole Williams revisits the 2001 MIT paper by Nelson Repenning and John Sterman that gave us the "capability trap." Their research found that every working hour goes either to producing output or to improving the process, and that managers under pressure push hours into output because it pays off immediately. Improvement pays off slowly and can look like failure at first, a pattern the authors call worse before better. Deferred maintenance, hidden problems and rewarded firefighting erode capability, which looks like a people problem and invites still more pressure, so staff work harder with less to show for it. The DuPont maintenance case illustrates the trap. Williams turns the paper into practice: plan production capacity and improvement capacity separately, schedule named improvement sessions, warn stakeholders of the dip, reinvest freed hours, and track time spent reworking work marked done.
points: Output rises at once when managers add pressure, while improvement pays back slowly, so the short-term incentive always favours working harder over working smarter.
The capability trap shows up as gradual decline that looks like a people problem, which prompts more pressure and speeds the erosion.
Expect a dip before improvement pays off, and tell stakeholders in advance that output will slow for a few weeks.
Plan production time and improvement time as separate resources, with improvement sessions that have a name, an owner and a date.
Rework on items already marked done is an early warning: if it grows each quarter, capability is eroding even when output looks fine.
quotes: According to Repenning and Sterman, applying pressure and working harder reads as a shortcut. Processes stay broken, training gets delayed, better tools aren’t selected because of time constraints and pressure from managers to accomplish the tasks.

However, working smart can look like failure at first. Improving a process takes time, and results come later. Better capability means less rework and fewer fires to put out. This frees time. Time to think. Those hours can go back into more improvement. The authors call this reinvestment. Repenning and Sterman describe this as worse before better. Managers should expect a dip before the process gets better.

The drop is gradual and doesn’t look like a structural problem. It looks like a people problem. The manager blames effort, so they apply pressure. People respond quickly by cutting more improvement to hit the number. The output rises for a while, which pleases the manager. Each round of this behavior erodes capability.
One says, there’s a problem, let’s fix it. The other says, we have a problem, someone is screwing up, let’s go beat them up.
Improvement capacity: time invested in making tomorrow’s work cleaner, faster, and less likely to need rework and the breakdown rate drops.
Keep track of time spent fixing work already marked as done. If the number increases each quarter, the capability may be eroding even when output looks fine.

Time is the one resource every project runs on. It’s also the easiest to spend badly. If you spend it all, capability wears down quickly. Protect some time for improvement, and it comes back with interest.
